v.why: Stepping up an already large learning rate causes divergence and large accuracy drops on all datasets (experiments 3, 10, 17).
Reducing a very large learning rate restores stable training, giving big gains (experiments 9, 18).
With a tiny learning rate 243 epochs underfit, so a larger step helps more than it does elsewhere (experiment 11).
Stepping up an already strong L2 penalty over-regularizes and hurts accuracy (experiments 84, 97).
Relaxing a strong L2 penalty frees capacity and improves accuracy (experiments 87, 93).
Extra L2 on top of an unstable high learning rate compounds training difficulty (experiment 82).
Wider networks with large learning rates have larger effective updates and are more prone to diverging (experiments 28, 22).
Deeper networks are less stable with large learning rates (experiments 45, 52).
Deep three-layer networks tolerate large learning rates poorly (experiments 7, 14).
Narrow networks are capacity-limited, so adding width helps more than it does for wide ones (experiment 29).

raw:
These hypotheses come from the 100 experiments plus general knowledge of MLP training. They are not verified against the full table. The strongest signal is that large learning rates (the high band) are unstable, so stepping the learning rate up hurts there and stepping it down helps (experiments 3, 9, 18, 10, 17). Large alpha (the high band) is also over-regularizing, so stepping alpha up hurts there (84, 97, 82).
